2611.10102.abstract: Although significant progress has been made over recent decades, a comprehensive and predictive framework for galaxy formation remains elusive. Starting from cosmological initial conditions, current models cannot a priori accurately predict key galaxy properties such as their structure, size, star formation histories, chemical abundance patterns, or supermassive black hole mass. This challenge stems from the vast range of spatial scales involved, as numerical simulations must simultaneously account for sub-AU processes nearby stars and black holes in addition to Mpc-scale cosmological gas inflows/outflows and environmental effects. Consequently, simulations must rely on subgrid models and approximations. As a result, theoretical progress in galaxy formation remains fundamentally driven by observational data and the iterative testing of model predictions against empirical results. Here we highlight five key open problems in theoretical galaxy formation that require dedicated observations of the high-redshift Universe, beyond what can currently be achieved through GO programs.

2611.10301.abstract: We present a spectroscopic database and analysis of satellite streaks in Public Data Release 1 (PDR1) from the Hobby-Eberly Telescope Dark Energy Experiment (HETDEX), covering 6778 observations and $\sim$90 deg$^2$ of sky from January 2017 to July 2024. We detect 527 streaks across 492 observations, a contamination fraction of 7.3% that rises to monthly values above 20% by 2023--2024, although the streaks mask only 0.09% of the survey area. Of the 527 streaks, 475 (90.1%) are identified with a cataloged object using archival two-line elements: 258 (54%) lie in low or Earth orbit and 217 (46%) are geostationary or highly elliptical. Only 35% were launched since 2010; the rest are spent rocket bodies, debris, and older spacecraft. This reflects HETDEX's sensitivity to faint objects and its 2017--2024 observing baseline. The Hobby-Eberly Telescope's large 10\,m aperture and HETDEX's $\sim$6\,minute exposures result in similar observed magnitudes for low Earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary Earth orbit (GEO) objects (median $g_{\rm AB}=16.2\pm1.1$ for LEO, $16.7\pm1.1$ for GEO). However, once transit time is corrected for, instantaneous magnitudes differ widely: $g_{\rm inst}=7.4$ for LEO versus $g_{\rm inst}=13.0$ for GEO objects, a difference of 5.6\,mag, while the exposure-averaged magnitudes differ by only 0.5 mag. Normalized to 550 km, the 34 Starlink streaks give $g(550 {\rm km})=5.95$, consistent with the mean $V(550\,{\rm km})=5.92\pm0.04$ reported for VisorSat-design spacecraft. The spectra are consistent with reflected sunlight, with modest, signal-to-noise-driven differences in slope. The catalog, spectra, and code are archived at this https URL.

2611.11159.abstract: The Polarimeter to Unify Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) is a very wide field polarizing imager covering a 90 degree diameter region of the sky, stitched together from four individual fields of view (FOVs), three of which are supported by Wide Field Imagers (WFIs) with 40 degree diameter individual FOVs. The science objective requires precise measurement of linear polarization. The WFI FOV is sufficiently wide that polarizer angles are foreshortened by projection effects relative to the line of sight of each pixel in the instrument, deviating from their nominal angular positions of -60, 0, and +60 degree relative to the instrument frame of reference. These angles are foreshortened by the very wide WFI field of view, changing their effective angle across the image plane - an effect that is analogous to similar challenges of polarimetric right/left channel separation in large-format 3D cinema, such as the IMAX format. Using a simple geometrical approach we estimated the perceived polarizer angle in the WFI FOV will vary by +/-2.5 degree for +/-60 degree and +/-3.5 degree for 0 degree polarizer angles. We present the effect of this deviation on the polarized brightness to be recorded by WFI, along with how optical distortion will shift the location of foreshortened angles. We also discuss the implications of this effect on upcoming technologies based on polarimetry across in wide fields.

2611.12183.abstract: High-contrast imaging for the direct detection of exoplanets is limited by stellar brightness and by wavefront errors. Coronagraphy and wavefront control reduce these effects and enable contrast levels compatible with current testbeds and future missions such as the Roman Space Telescope. Within this framework, the MITHiC testbed at the Laboratoire d'Astrophysique de Marseille is being upgraded with a new deformable mirror used to control the wavefront. It complements the existing setup, which includes a classic Lyot coronagraph and a spatial light modulator (SLM) enabling phase and amplitude control to optimize the dark-hole region. We also implement the Zernike wavefront sensor (ZELDA) to correct low-order aberrations. This contribution presents recent progress on the MITHiC upgrade and initial results, highlighting its role as a versatile platform for developing advanced high-contrast imaging techniques.

2611.12704.abstract: The FRAM (F/Photometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescopes can measure the aerosol extinction at optical wavelengths using wide-field stellar photometry at the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) sites. The Angstrom exponent describes the wavelength dependence of aerosol extinction. In this work we extend the FRAM method from a single $B$-filter (440 nm) analysis using the Tycho-2 catalogue to a simultaneous three-filter analysis in $B$, $V$, and $R$ (440, 540, and 620 nm) using Gaia DR3 synthetic photometry, which provides photometry directly in the Johnson--Cousins system without passband transformations. The exponent is derived from the vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) for the B--V, V--R, and B--R filter pairs at three sites over 2021--2022. The multi-filter VAOD shows a systematic filter-dependent ordering that is inconsistent with physical expectation and produces negative exponents. It is not currently possible to determine which filter yields the correct VAOD, and none of the four processing configurations we tested resolves the ordering. We introduce an intercept correction as a practical remedy that yields physically plausible exponents. At the two southern Paranal sites (CTAO-S0 and CTAO-S1) the exponent distributions are unimodal, with mean $\alpha \approx 0.84$ (B--V) and $0.65$ (B--R) at CTAO-S0 and $0.60$ and $0.41$ at CTAO-S1. At CTAO-N (La Palma) the distributions are bimodal, with $\alpha \approx 0.2$ (B--V) during episodic Saharan dust intrusions and $\alpha \approx 1.3$ under clean background conditions. AERONET sun-photometer measurements on the dates common to both instruments show the same two populations, providing qualitative support for the FRAM method.

2611.10127.abstract: We present a resolved star study of AM-1, a distant ($D \simeq 120$ kpc), faint ($M_V \sim -5.1$) Milky Way (MW) globular cluster, based on Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) imaging. To perform photometry of the Euclid VIS and NISP imaging, we develop a Euclid-specific module for the crowded field stellar photometry package DOLPHOT. We construct and present empirical point spread function (PSF) models for VIS and NISP, along with a photometric calibration, entirely from the public Q1 images. Our photometry reaches $5\sigma$ point source depths of $I_E, Y_E, J_E, H_E = 27.1, 25.3, 25.5, 25.3$, $\sim$1-1.5 mag deeper than the public Q1 catalog, as expected for dedicated resolved star PSF photometry. We resolve the cluster to $\sim$1 mag below its main sequence turnoff in all bands. The Euclid photometry agrees with color-magnitude diagram (CMD) modeling of archival HST/WFPC2 imaging and with the 2MASS-anchored VISTA Hemisphere Survey to $\lesssim0.02$ mag in $I_E$, $J_E$, and $H_E$, with a $\sim$0.07 mag offset in $Y_E$. We find that AM-1 hosts an old ($\sim$10.6 Gyr), intermediate-metallicity ([Fe/H] $\sim -1$) population, with a present-day stellar mass of $\sim 2\times10^4\,M_\odot$ and $M/L_V \simeq 2.2$, and has a half-light radius of $\sim$12-16 pc with a round, low-concentration profile. These affirm earlier studies placing AM-1 among the most extended, diffuse outer-halo clusters, which dynamical work identifies as accreted. We describe and publicly release DOLPHOT v2.1, the Euclid module, and its empirical PSFs, which together enable Euclid resolved star studies ranging from faint MW systems such as AM-1 to more luminous galaxies throughout the Local Volume. We anticipate further refinements, including spatially varying PSFs, with Euclid Data Release 1.

2611.10320.abstract: We present an approach for numerical simulations of pure radiation fluids within the general relativistic hydrodynamics framework. The approach models radiation as a self-gravitating perfect fluid with vanishing rest mass, enabling simulations of radiation fluids in strong-gravity spacetimes. Building on the existing relativistic hydrodynamics code Whisky, within the Einstein Toolkit framework, we introduce modifications to incorporate radiation fluids, including updates to the source terms, recovery scheme, and Riemann solvers. Modifications are validated using standard shock tube tests. We present results for radiation accretion onto a single black hole, as well as a photon star solution for radiation in unstable hydrostatic equilibrium, demonstrating both collapse and dispersion under perturbations.

2611.10342.abstract: Detection and characterization of Earth-like worlds is a primary science goal for the upcoming NASA flagship Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The HWO mission will be the first of its kind to specifically search for Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars and characterize their atmospheres to identify potential biosignatures. A mission with such ambitious science goals thus requires equally robust and physically realistic simulation tools. In this work, we extend the realism of the EXOSIMS framework by incorporating phase-dependent biosignature detectability. We use the spectral retrieval tool rfast to determine the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) required to detect atmospheric O2 and H2O as a function of planetary phase and incorporate these requirements directly into EXOSIMS characterization integration-time calculations. Although the required molecular detection SNR decreases toward increasingly crescent phases, successful molecular detections are concentrated at intermediate phase angles, demonstrating the competing effects of molecular information content and direct-imaging observability. Relative to fixed characterization thresholds of SNR = 5 for H2O and SNR = 8.5 for O2, the phase-dependent treatment increases mean molecular detection yield by 76.8 percent for H2O and 29.7 percent for O2. Ultimately, we provide a framework that improves simulation fidelity, increases the realism of EXOSIMS as we expand to assess additional biosignatures in future work, and marries detection and characterization in yield modeling as we look to the future with HWO.

2611.10456.abstract: The transition from atomic hydrogen (HI) to molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) is the first step in the evolution from diffuse interstellar gas to dense star-forming cores. HI narrow self-absorption (HINSA), produced by cold atomic gas mixed with molecular material, provides a direct tracer of the HI-to-H$_2$ transition in molecular clouds. Existing HINSA analyses typically model HINSA as a single Gaussian component with a uniform spin temperature. This approach cannot recover the radial HI distribution and yields large errors for young cores whose profiles deviate from a Gaussian shape. Here we present hinspheres, an open-source framework that models the core as onion-like spherically symmetric concentric shells, solves radiative transfer along the line of sight and jointly fits the HI abundance, temperature, and kinematic parameters. The framework recovers all parameters with a mean relative error of 4.6-6.8% on our synthetic data with different ages. A combined resolution-noise grid shows that the median recovery error remains below 16% for cores within 1 kpc observed at FAST resolution with noise levels below 0.2 K. Applying it to the dark cores L1574 and L1544, we reveal radial HI abundance profiles that span about three orders of magnitude, which were missed by the single-Gaussian method. The derived chemical ages are $6.5\times10^6$ and $8.7\times10^6$ yr, respectively. Compared with the commonly used single-Gaussian method, hinspheres characterizes the radial profile of HINSA structures more accurately, making it well suited to identifying and analyzing young cores undergoing the HI-to-H$_2$ transition.

2611.11075.abstract: We investigate possible causal influences in five historical seasons (1989-1993) of NGC 5548 using a version of the Synergistic-Unique-Redundant Decomposition (SURD) method adapted for this analysis, an information-theoretic causal discovery method for time series. Two four-variable sets contain the blue wing (B), core (C) and red wing (R) of H-beta together with either total H-beta (H) or the 5100 Angstrom continuum (F). We examine 7200 decompositions with common and unequal lags, two or three seasonal flux states, and base delays of 1-30 d. We rank the individual named components within each information family, reporting their amplitudes and simultaneous leakage. In 1989, unique continuum information about the core reaches 0.799 and 0.387 of target entropy for two and three states, with leakage 0.047 and 0.276. In 1992, the red-wing history supplies unique information about the future blue wing in both variable sets and both state counts, with peak target-entropy fractions 0.106-0.166. Distinct joint influences also emerge: for the 1991 core, the two-state S(F,B) and S(F,R) components contribute 0.187 and 0.125 at 20 d with leakage 0.087, although the unique continuum term vanishes. Strong core-wing redundancy identifies candidate inputs for simpler predictive models. Large late-lag leakage, reaching approximately 0.97 in the total set, identifies targets for additional driver measurements and richer temporal histories. The resulting seasonal map of individual, shared and joint influences complements the response delays and velocity structure measured by reverberation mapping, and provides specific causal hypotheses for the evolving broad-line region.

2611.11922.abstract: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) pose a major challenge to Bayesian parameter inference because of their complex, highly multimodal likelihood surfaces. Locating narrow high-likelihood regions is particularly difficult without knowledge of the true source parameters, which is unavailable in real observations. We develop a deep-learning-assisted Bayesian inference framework that combines neural-network-guided parameter-space localization, particle swarm optimization, and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Applied to simulated six-month EMRI signals, the framework recovers posterior distributions in close agreement with reference MCMC analyses initialized near the true parameter values, without requiring such knowledge for initialization. Once the neural network has been trained, the complete inference pipeline takes approximately 10 hours per signal.

2611.12158.abstract: Millimetre-to-centimetre orbital debris poses a hazard to spacecraft, but its abundance remains difficult to measure. Spaceborne radars offer a substantial sensitivity advantage at close range: received echo power decreases with the fourth power of distance, so an otherwise identical object ten times closer produces a 10,000 times stronger echo. We investigate this opportunity using openly available Sentinel-1 radar voltages recorded on six calendar days. Catalogue-assisted processing identifies a manually validated sample of 76 objects at ranges of 41.7--492.9 km, including satellites, rocket bodies and debris fragments. A blind search recovers two selected debris transits without using their orbital predictions during detection. A short debris encounter also demonstrates how precise range and Doppler measurements can refine a catalogue orbit. Ground scatter increases the effective background and is the principal sensitivity limitation in Earth-looking observations. An ideal receiver-noise sensitivity comparison predicts detectable conducting-sphere diameters of approximately 3.4 mm for Sentinel-1 and 0.6 mm for EarthCARE at 10 km range, assuming coherent integration limited by beam transit time and a 10 ms cap. These results establish the feasibility of space-object detection using existing Earth-observation radars and motivate statistical debris surveys and targeted orbit refinement following collision warnings. Observations directed away from Earth and receive windows adapted to nearby objects could improve sensitivity to small debris.

2611.12179.abstract: The microhertz gravitational wave (GW) frequency regime remains one of the least explored regions of the GW spectrum. This is due to the physical limitations of our current and upcoming GW observatories such as LIGO and LISA, which are tuned to dHz and mHz respectively. Proposed experiments targeting the $\mu$Hz regime are ambitious, expensive and unlikely to be operational within the next 20 years. Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs), with their Galaxy-sized baselines, occupy the other end of the spectrum; the frequencies they are sensitive to are a function of the observing cadence and total dataset timespan. Existing PTA campaigns have cadences and timespans corresponding to the nanohertz regime, however the possibility exists that they can be 'pushed' to detect higher frequencies. This paper investigates the viability of a custom microhertz-sensitive PTA, observing a small number of millisecond pulsars with a daily cadence, over the course of 1 and 2 years respectively. We assume the use of both 100-m and 500-m class radio telescopes for these observations, and an idealised noise model with negligible systematics to determine the most optimistic detection threshold. We compute the sensitivity of our proposed high-cadence PTA configurations to power-law signals and individual GW sources. We find that a 500-m class telescope would likely be able to set new upper limits on individual sources and GW background signals in the $0.1-1~\mu$Hz range; while a 100-m class telescope would, in the best case, only match that of the performance of the EPTA second data release in the same range. Finally we consider a possible $\mu$Hz PTA consisting of SKA-Mid and DSA observing 24 pulsars; we find this performs on par with the 500-m class while using far less telescope time, presenting a more feasible solution to microhertz-GW pulsar timing.

2611.12808.abstract: Xenoscope is a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operated at the University of Zurich to investigate electron transport over distances relevant to the next-generation XLZD (XENON-LUX-ZEPLIN-DARWIN) observatory. We demonstrate electron drift over $2.6$ m in liquid xenon using cosmic-muon-induced ionization signals. External muon tagging provides a timing reference for charge produced at known depths, while the endpoint of the average electroluminescence waveform probes transport over the full drift length. We measure electron drift velocities of $(1.320 \pm 0.006)$ mm/$\mu$s at $(80.92 \pm 0.36)$ V/cm and $(1.436 \pm 0.001)$ mm/$\mu$s at $(96.00 \pm 0.42)$ V/cm. These results establish detectable charge transport over meter-scale distances and provide an experimental benchmark for the development of future large liquid-xenon time projection chambers.

2611.12841.abstract: We present uniform posteriors indicating the presence or absence of stellar and planetary companions over a sample of $10^5$ stars in Hipparcos and Gaia. We use the "G23H" catalog to fit a model that incorporates absolute astrometry constraints from Hipparcos, Gaia DR2, and Gaia DR3, as well as Gaia DR3 photometry, excess RV variability, and includes information from the presence or absence of common-proper motion companions. The resulting posteriors can be used directly to detect new companions, to target RV and imaging follow-up observations, and for downstream demographics studies. We highlight example detections of known and new candidate companions and the companion detection rate across the HR diagram. The modelling approach we present is directly applicable to Gaia DR4 epoch astrometry and RVs. All posteriors are provided as a machine-readable catalog and user-accessible website this http URL.

2611.12846.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission is a powerful tool for the study of the interstellar medium (ISM) in both Galactic and extragalactic contexts. It can reveal ionization state, radiation field, metallicity, composition, and ISM structure as sculpted by processes like turbulence and stellar feedback. Here we use NASA's SPHEREx to produce clean, high-resolution PAH maps at spectral resolution R $\sim$ 35 (compared to WISE at R $\sim$ 2). Prior treatments of the SPHEREx linear variable filter data seek to convert them to more conventional band-averaged maps that can leave striping artifacts associated with spatially variable wavelength sampling, especially at emission lines. In contrast, we deliver a scalable forward-modeling method capable of generating high-quality all-sky SPHEREx emission-line maps at 8.5 arcsec FWHM angular resolution (on 6.4 arcsec pixels), while naturally producing maps without visible striping. We reformat the data into a pixel-level database, mask stellar contamination, and infill missing pixels with a conditional, data-driven, anisotropic Gaussian process. We apply our method to produce 3.3 $\mu$m and 3.4 $\mu$m PAH and Paschen-$\alpha$ emission maps of a set of fields spanning a range of Galactic and extragalactic conditions including the Rosette nebula, the Corona Australis molecular cloud, M33, and M31. We demonstrate the quality and synergies of our SPHEREx 3.3 $\mu$m PAH maps by comparisons with other available gas and dust tracer maps and achieve sensitivities up to $\sigma(I_{3.3}) = 2.7 \times 10^{-8}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$. We estimate that a two-year extension of the SPHEREx survey, with modest modifications to the scanning strategy, would match or exceed the PAH sensitivity of WISE over the whole sky.

2611.12849.abstract: The Tierras Observatory is a fully robotic 1.3-m telescope at the Fred Lawrence Whipple Observatory in southern Arizona. Tierras achieves sub-part-per-thousand (ppt) photometric precision on two timescales: intra-night, to detect and characterize transits of planets around nearby mid-to-late M dwarfs, and night-to-night across an observing season, to characterize the long-term variability of their host stars. We describe the facility and instrument design, our photometric pipeline, and our on-sky performance. We present the first ground-based light curves with sub-ppt precision over timescales of months. This precision enables a range of exoplanet-related science, including the measurement of host star rotation periods, the detection of long-period transits, and the discovery of additional terrestrial planets in known M dwarf systems.
